data.name: VectorWave
data.detailed_description:
Hi Everyone, Thanks for your support over the years. As one of the only two people behind VectorWave I would like to thank everyone who ever downloaded my game from the bottom of my heart. I've been making plans to revive this game for over 2 years. I've wanted to update it to modern controllers/headsets, even give it a minor graphical facelift, but unfortunately my time is very limited. As of now, VectorWave is dead. You can only play it if you have an original HTC Vive or a first or second gen oculus. This bring me no joy, but after 2 years of attempting to get the time to work on it, I believe it's finally time to throw in the towel. Any free time I get will go towards new game ideas of endeavors I may have. Thanks again.

VectorWave translates the traditional tower defense experience into virtual reality, allowing you the freedom to buy, place, toss, and move towers as you see fit between each wave with almost no need for menus. Each hand serves its own purpose in your efforts to build an impenetrable defense grid against increasingly difficult hordes of malware bent on destroying your mainframe.

Moving from a 2-D top down perspective in traditional TD games to Virtual Reality allows us to expand on this genre like never before. Because split second decisions and positioning matter, VectorWave's simple, yet versatile, movement and scaling system allows you to either stand directly in the action, or watch your carefully laid out plans from afar.

Current Game Features


  • 21 Levels
  • 20 Enemy Types
  • 22 Towers
  • Unique Player Abilities
  • Achievements
  • Global Leader-boards
  • Trading Cards

Planned Features


  • Level Editor
  • Challenge Mode
  • Endless Mode

Game currently supports the HTC Vive and the Oculus Rift



Demo Details


We included a Demo you could try before you purchase the full product.
We understand that it is important for the consumer to know what they are buying.
The demo is just a small slice of the finished game that we feel represents VectorWave well.
Many more features are included in the full version.

Demo Features


  • 7 Unique Levels
  • 10 Enemy Types
  • 10 Towers

All music tracks heard in this game were provided by the generous Zachary Kemp.
Check out his Work Here:


Physics and Interaction engine provided by the lovely people over at NewtonVR.
Check out them here:

reviews.review:
VectorWave approaches the familiar tower defense formula from a perspective that feels especially appropriate for virtual reality. Instead of managing defenses through a conventional overhead interface, the game places the battlefield directly in front of the player and encourages physical interaction with its components. Developed and published by Fizzure Entertainment, it combines strategic tower placement with motion-controlled manipulation, allowing players to grab, position, and move defensive structures while enemy forces advance toward the mainframe. It is a straightforward concept, but the VR implementation gives ordinary tower defense mechanics a much more tactile personality.

The objective revolves around protecting a central mainframe from successive waves of hostile malware. Players purchase and deploy towers across the battlefield, building defensive arrangements capable of dealing with different types of approaching enemies. One of the game's most enjoyable ideas is the ability to manipulate the scale and perspective of the battlefield. Pulling back provides a useful overview of the entire defensive network, while moving closer makes individual towers and enemy encounters easier to observe. This creates the sensation of controlling an interactive miniature battlefield rather than simply watching units move around a flat strategy map.

Content variety gives the campaign a reasonable amount of substance. There are 21 levels to overcome, accompanied by 20 enemy types and 22 different towers. Having more than twenty defensive options encourages experimentation, particularly when later encounters demand stronger combinations rather than simply filling available space with the same reliable tower. Enemies also vary enough to make positioning and tower selection meaningful. The addition of player abilities introduces another active element, allowing the player to become more directly involved instead of relying exclusively on automated defenses.

The physical controls are arguably the defining feature. Picking up and repositioning towers makes battlefield management feel immediate, and the ability to toss objects around adds a playful quality rarely associated with traditional tower defense games. These interactions can turn moments of pressure into frantic physical problem solving as the player attempts to repair weaknesses in a defensive layout before enemies break through. It is an inventive way of translating a strategy genre into VR because the headset and motion controllers influence how the game is played rather than merely changing how it is viewed.

Visually, VectorWave has a relatively simple digital aesthetic that suits its computer-themed setting. The environments, enemies, and towers prioritize readability over elaborate detail, which is sensible for a strategy game where players need to understand what is happening across several areas simultaneously. Its presentation clearly reflects the period in which it was developed, so players accustomed to newer VR releases should expect something more modest. The soundtrack contributes energy to the action, while the clean presentation generally keeps attention focused on managing the battlefield.

Replay value comes from improving strategies, experimenting with different defensive configurations, pursuing achievements, and competing through global leaderboards. The variety of towers provides opportunities to revisit levels with alternative approaches rather than following one rigid solution. At the same time, some originally envisioned additions never became part of the finished experience. Features such as a level editor, Challenge Mode, and Endless Mode were planned during development but were not ultimately delivered. Their absence limits the game's long-term potential, especially for players who would have enjoyed building custom scenarios or surviving increasingly difficult unrestricted waves.

The largest concern today is hardware support. VectorWave belongs to an earlier era of consumer VR and was designed around equipment such as the original HTC Vive and early Oculus hardware. Development has ended, and modernization for newer VR controllers and headsets was not completed. Consequently, players using contemporary VR equipment may encounter compatibility problems. This matters considerably more than the game's relatively modest PC hardware requirements because owning a powerful modern computer does not guarantee that its VR control implementation will function properly with newer equipment.

Steam Deck compatibility is effectively unsupported for practical gameplay. VectorWave is fundamentally a room-scale virtual reality title that depends on a compatible VR headset and tracked motion controllers. The Steam Deck by itself cannot reproduce the intended control system or VR environment, so this should not be considered a conventional handheld experience. Even if technical workarounds could theoretically be attempted with additional hardware, VectorWave is not designed as a native Steam Deck game and should be treated as incompatible with normal handheld play.

Despite those limitations, there is genuine creativity behind the project. Tower defense translates naturally into virtual reality because the battlefield already resembles a miniature model that players want to observe and manipulate. VectorWave capitalizes on this by turning tower placement into a physical activity and allowing the player to examine the action from different perspectives. The result demonstrates how VR can reshape an established genre without abandoning the strategic principles that originally made it enjoyable.

Its biggest weakness is ultimately age rather than concept. The 21 levels, 22 towers, 20 enemy types, physical interactions, abilities, achievements, and leaderboard features provide a respectable amount of material, but discontinued development and legacy hardware requirements substantially narrow its modern audience. Players who still possess compatible older VR equipment can discover an enjoyable and inventive tower defense experience, while owners of current hardware should approach it cautiously because compatibility cannot be assumed.

Its interactive approach to tower defense, respectable selection of defensive tools, varied enemies, and clever use of VR make it more ambitious than a simple virtual reality novelty. Its lasting appeal is held back by abandoned development, missing planned features, outdated VR compatibility, and the lack of meaningful Steam Deck support. As an early VR strategy experiment, however, it remains an interesting example of how traditional gameplay can become considerably more physical when reconstructed around virtual reality.

Rating: 7/10
